question: Is either of these true: the 2024 return these figures come from was a joint return, and for 2025 you are not filing a joint return with the same spouse (for example after a divorce, a separation or the death of your spouse in 2024); or, on this 2025 joint return, you and your spouse each filed a separate 2024 return whose Schedule D line 21 showed a loss?

findings.situation: A filer who filed jointly for 2024 and not jointly with that spouse for 2025 (for example, after a divorce) has no 2024 capital loss carryover because the 2024 Schedule D line 21 was not a loss, yet must answer YES and is refused.
findings.irs_text: Question: "the 2024 return these figures come from was a joint return, and for 2025 you are not filing a joint return with the same spouse". i1040sd p. 10: "if your 2024 Schedule D, line 21, is a loss and... Otherwise, you don't have any carryovers."
findings.why: The first limb has no loss or carryover condition, unlike the second limb, so it catches filers with nothing to allocate. The tool correctly computes a zero carryover for them, and the spouse-allocation rule has no effect.

findings.situation: A filer who filed jointly for 2024 and not jointly with that spouse for 2025 actually had the entire loss behind the joint carryover, yet must answer YES and is refused.
findings.irs_text: Question: "the 2024 return these figures come from was a joint return, and for 2025 you are not filing a joint return with the same spouse". i1040sd p. 10: "any capital loss carryover from the joint return can be deducted only on the return of the spouse who actually had the loss."
findings.why: When all of the loss belongs to the filer, the whole carryover figured from the joint return's amounts is deductible on the filer's return, so no allocation is needed. The worksheet computation is therefore correct, but the question's wording still forces a refusal.

question: Does the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents, or parents who lived apart (including parents who never married), apply to this person, for example because a Form 8332 release or a decree lets the noncustodial parent claim the child? Answer yes whether you are the custodial parent who signed the release (or whose decree or agreement lets the other parent claim the child) or the noncustodial parent using it.

findings.situation: A custodial parent has a post-2008 decree or agreement saying the other parent may claim the child, but has signed no Form 8332 or substantially similar statement.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "If the divorce decree or separation agreement went into effect after 2008, the noncustodial parent can't include pages from the decree or agreement instead of Form 8332." Question: "(or whose decree or agreement lets the other parent claim the child)"
findings.why: The wording makes this filer answer YES because the decree says the other parent may claim the child, yet condition 4 is not met and the special rule does not apply. The tool's ordinary Step 1 test would treat the child correctly as the custodial parent's qualifying child, so the refusal is unnecessary. A post-1984, pre-2009 decree that makes the claim conditional, such as on paying support, raises the same problem.

findings.situation: A release or decree exists, but another condition of the special rule fails, such as the parents living together during the last 6 months of 2025 or the parents not providing over half of the child's support.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "if all of the following conditions apply. 1. The parents are divorced, legally separated, separated under a written separation agreement, or lived apart at all times during the last 6 months of 2025... 2. The child received over half of the child's support for 2025 from the parents... 3. The child is in custody of one or both of the parents for more than half of 2025." Question: "parents who lived apart"; "for example because a Form 8332 release or a decree lets the noncustodial parent claim the child"
findings.why: The question does not state the 6-month period, the support test, or the custody test, and its example suggests that a release alone triggers the rule. A custodial filer would answer YES and be refused even though the rule does not apply and the tool computes the child correctly.

findings.situation: A divorced, separated, or never-married custodial parent has not released the claim, and no decree or agreement lets the other parent claim the child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent... if all of the following conditions apply." Question: "Does the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents, or parents who lived apart (including parents who never married), apply to this person"
findings.why: The rule's name and the question's parenthetical can be read to mean that the parents' status alone makes the rule apply, which leads to YES. The example points to NO, which is the correct answer because the tool computes this common case correctly.

findings.situation: A custodial parent signed a Form 8332 only for a year other than 2025, or revoked an earlier release so that it no longer applies to 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "they won't claim the child as a dependent for 2025"; "A custodial parent who has revoked their previous release of a claim to certain tax benefits for a child must include a copy of the revocation with their return." Question: "the custodial parent who signed the release"
findings.why: The question names no tax year and does not mention revocation, so this filer could read "signed the release" as YES even though no release applies to 2025. A filer who answers NO after a revocation gets the computed line with no prompt to attach the required copy.

findings.situation: A filer who is neither parent, such as a grandparent or aunt, lives with the child and the custodial parent, and the custodial parent has released the claim to the noncustodial parent.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "If conditions (1) through (4) apply, only the noncustodial parent can claim the child for purposes of the child tax credit and credit for other dependents (lines 19 and 28)." Question: "Answer yes whether you are the custodial parent who signed the release... or the noncustodial parent using it."
findings.why: The first sentence asks whether the rule applies to the child, which would be YES, but the last sentence names only the two parents, so a third-party filer could read the rule as not reaching them and answer NO. The tool would then compute the child as this filer's qualifying child even though the release bars the filer from claiming the child for those credits.

question: Is this person a child who, at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn't a member of your family or the child's family (even if the child has since been returned)?

findings.situation: A child disappeared in mid-2025, but law enforcement did not presume a non-family kidnapping until early 2026, before the return was filed, so the months-lived count could fall to 6 or fewer.
findings.irs_text: "The child is presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn't a member of your family or the child's family." (p501, 2025, p. 13); "In the year the kidnapping occurred, the child lived with you for more than half of the part of the year before the date of the kidnapping." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The IRS text ties the year to when the kidnapping occurred and sets no deadline for the presumption, but the question asks whether the child was presumed kidnapped "at any time during 2025." This filer could truthfully answer NO, and the tool would then compute the residency lines as false even though the kidnapped-child treatment may apply.

findings.situation: A child was presumed kidnapped for a few days in 2025, was returned, and lived with the filer for well over six months anyway.
findings.irs_text: Question: "at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped ... (even if the child has since been returned)"; IRS: "To meet this test, your child must have lived with you for more than half the year." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The filer must answer YES, but the child meets the residency test on actual time lived, so the months count gives the correct result. The tool refuses a case it computes correctly.

findings.situation: A child was presumed kidnapped during 2025 but did not live with the filer for more than half of the part of the year before the kidnapping, or for more than half of the part of the year after the child's return.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Is this person a child who, at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped"; IRS: "You can treat your child as meeting the residency test even if the child has been kidnapped, but the following statements must be true." followed by statements 2 and 3 on time lived before the kidnapping and after the return (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The question tests only statement 1, so the filer answers YES even though the special treatment is unavailable. The ordinary months count, which the tool computes, would correctly apply if the child also fell short of more than half the year.

findings.situation: A child still presumed kidnapped during 2025 is past the end of the special treatment because the child would have reached age 18, or there was a determination of death, in an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: Question: "at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped"; IRS: "This treatment applies for all years until the earlier of: 1. The year there is a determination that the child is dead, or 2. The year the child would have reached age 18." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The question has no age or death cutoff, so a filer with a continuing presumption answers YES after the treatment has ended. The ordinary months count would correctly decide these lines, so the refusal is unnecessary.

findings.situation: The person presumed kidnapped was 18 or older, or was a relative such as a sibling, niece, or nephew rather than the filer's own child.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Is this person a child"; IRS: "You can treat your child as meeting the residency test even if the child has been kidnapped" (p501, 2025, p. 13); "To meet this test, a child must be: Your son, daughter, stepchild, or foster child, or a descendant ... Your brother, sister, half brother, half sister, stepbrother, or stepsister, or a descendant" (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: "A child" could mean a minor, the filer's own offspring, or anyone who fits the qualifying-child relationship test. Filers in the same situation could therefore answer differently, and the question does not say which meaning applies.

question: Was this person married at the end of 2025 (a person legally separated under a decree of divorce or separate maintenance is not married), or is a joint return being filed for 2025 that includes this person (including one filed by this person with a spouse who died during 2025, or by this person's surviving spouse after this person died during 2025)?

findings.situation: A person who was married at the end of 2025 and either files no joint return or files one only to claim a refund must answer YES, so the tool refuses the qualifying child and qualifying relative lines even though it computes them correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Was this person married at the end of 2025..." IRS: "if the person is married but doesn't file a joint return or files a joint return only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid, you may be able to claim that person as a dependent... In that case, go to Step 2, question 3 (for a qualifying child), or Step 4, question 4 (for a qualifying relative)." (i1040gi 2025 p. 21, Married person)
findings.why: Marriage alone does not change either test, and the Married person rule returns this case to the ordinary flow. The qualifying child line already has a helper for a joint return filed other than only to claim a refund, and the qualifying relative conditions at Step 4 do not depend on marital status, so the refusal is unnecessary for these two lines. It remains needed for the EIC line, which does not compute the dependency test that a married child must meet (i1040gi p. 44).

findings.situation: A person whose spouse died during 2025, who was therefore not married at the end of 2025, and who files a joint return only to claim a refund must answer YES, so the tool refuses all three lines even though it computes them correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or is a joint return being filed for 2025 that includes this person (including one filed by this person with a spouse who died during 2025...)" IRS: "Who isn't filing a joint return for 2025 or is filing a joint return for 2025 only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid" (i1040gi 2025 pp. 17, 41); "A child who was married at the end of 2025 is a qualifying child only if..." (i1040gi 2025 p. 44, Married child)
findings.why: The joint-return clause has no exception for a return filed only to claim a refund, but the IRS text treats that return as passing the joint-return test. The Married child dependency limit does not apply because the person was not married at year-end, so the computed EIC line is also correct on these facts.

question: Did you and others together provide over half of this person's support for 2025, with no one person providing over half (a multiple support situation), whether you or another contributor claims the person?

findings.situation: A noncustodial parent can claim a child as a qualifying relative under Form 8332 or a qualifying decree, although the parent did not personally provide over half of the child's support and no multiple support situation exists.
findings.irs_text: "For whom you provided over half of the person's support in 2025. But see Children of divorced or separated parents, Multiple support agreements, and Kidnapped child, later." (i1040gi 2025 p. 19); "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent" (i1040gi 2025 p. 20)
findings.why: The computed line requires that the filer provided over half of the support, and this question asks only about multiple support, so the parent truthfully answers NO. Unless another screen not shown here catches this case, the tool wrongly computes that the child is not a qualifying relative.

findings.situation: A child presumed kidnapped by a nonfamily member may be taken into account under special rules that the question does not mention.
findings.irs_text: "But see Children of divorced or separated parents, Multiple support agreements, and Kidnapped child, later." (i1040gi 2025 p. 19); "you may be able to take the child into account in determining your eligibility for... the credit for other dependents" (i1040gi 2025 p. 21)
findings.why: A parent in this situation truthfully answers NO because the question asks only about shared support. The computed conditions show no kidnapped-child exception, so the tool may wrongly deny qualifying relative status.

findings.situation: A permanently and totally disabled person has sheltered workshop income that may be excluded from the gross income test, bringing countable income under $5,200.
findings.irs_text: "If your relative... is permanently and totally disabled (defined later), certain income for services performed at a sheltered workshop may be excluded for this test." (i1040gi 2025 p. 20)
findings.why: The question does not address gross income, so the filer truthfully answers NO. If the helper "Gross income under $5,200" is answered using total gross income, the tool wrongly computes that the person is not a qualifying relative.

findings.situation: The person is not the filer's qualifying child but is the qualifying child of another taxpayer, which disqualifies the person as a qualifying relative.
findings.irs_text: "Who wasn't a qualifying child (see Step 1) of any taxpayer for 2025." (i1040gi 2025 p. 19)
findings.why: The helper label "Qualifying child (Step 1)" does not show that it tests for a qualifying child of any taxpayer, and this question does not ask. If the helper tests only the filer, the filer truthfully answers NO and the tool may wrongly compute qualifying relative status.

findings.situation: A filer contributes to shared support in a multiple support situation, but another contributor claims the person, so the filer correctly cannot treat the person as a qualifying relative.
findings.irs_text: Question: "whether you or another contributor claims the person"; IRS: "special rules may apply that would treat you as having provided over half of the support" (i1040gi 2025 p. 21)
findings.why: The wording requires YES even when the filer is not claiming the person and is not treated as providing over half. On a NO path, the tool's false result on "You provided over half" would be correct, so the refusal is unnecessary.

findings.situation: Support is shared with no one providing over half, but the person fails another qualifying relative test, such as having gross income of $5,200 or more or being outside the listed relationships and household rule.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Did you and others together provide over half of this person's support for 2025, with no one person providing over half"; IRS: "Who had gross income of less than $5,200 in 2025." (i1040gi 2025 p. 19)
findings.why: The question makes the filer answer YES based on support alone, even though the person fails another required condition. The tool could correctly compute false for that condition, so the refusal is unnecessary.

findings.situation: A filer may be unsure whether "others" includes the person being supported or a government or other public source, such as when the filer and one of those sources together provide over half of the support.
findings.irs_text: Question: "you and others together"; IRS: "If no one person contributed over half of the support of your relative... but you and another person(s) provided more than half of your relative's support" (i1040gi 2025 p. 21)
findings.why: Neither the question nor the quoted IRS text says which contributors count as "others" or "another person(s)", and the details are left to Pub. 501. Filers with the same facts could reasonably answer either YES or NO, which determines whether the tool refuses or computes the line.

question: Does this person meet the conditions to be the qualifying child of any other person for 2025, under the dependent rules or under the EIC rules (which have no support test)?

findings.situation: A custodial parent has released the claim to the child on Form 8332, and the noncustodial parent, with whom the child did not live for more than half of 2025, claims the child.
findings.irs_text: "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent... only the noncustodial parent can claim the child for purposes of the child tax credit and credit for other dependents" (i1040gi 2025, p. 20); see also "unless the special rule for Children of divorced or separated parents... applies" (p. 21).
findings.why: The noncustodial parent fails the lived-with test and is only treated as having a qualifying child, so the custodial filer can truthfully answer NO to "meet the conditions." The tool then computes dependent.qualifying_child as true for a filer who has released the claim, and the question also does not catch a noncustodial filer whose line computes false on the lived-with helper.

findings.situation: A child who was married at the end of 2025 and is not filing a joint return lives with the filer, but the filer cannot claim the child as a dependent and the divorced-or-separated-parents exception does not apply.
findings.irs_text: "If the child was married, see Married child, later" (i1040gi 2025, p. 41); "A child who was married at the end of 2025 is a qualifying child only if (a) you can claim the child as your dependent, or (b) you could have claimed the child as your dependent except for the special rule for Children of divorced or separated parents" (p. 44).
findings.why: The question asks only about other people's claims, so a filer can truthfully answer NO when no one else qualifies. The computed dependent.eic_child has no married-child condition and returns true for a child the text excludes.

findings.situation: The child lives with the filer and another person and provided over half of their own support, so the child fails the support test for dependent.qualifying_child but meets the EIC conditions for the other person.
findings.irs_text: Question: "under the dependent rules or under the EIC rules (which have no support test)"; IRS: "Who didn't provide over half of their own support for 2025" (i1040gi 2025, p. 17).
findings.why: The EIC branch forces YES, which also refuses dependent.qualifying_child. That line would correctly compute false from the support helper without any tie-breaker, because the child is not a dependent-rule qualifying child of anyone.

findings.situation: The filer is the child's only parent among the eligible claimants, such as a parent living with the child and the filer's own parent, so the tie-breaker necessarily resolves in the filer's favor.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Does this person meet the conditions to be the qualifying child of any other person for 2025"; IRS: "If only one of the persons is the child's parent, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parent" and "you can claim Lee as a qualifying child" (i1040gi 2025, pp. 21, 44).
findings.why: The filer must truthfully answer YES and is refused, although the tool's computed true result is the correct outcome. This over-refusal is conservative, but it does block a case the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: Another person meets the qualifying-child tests on paper but will not or need not claim the child, for example because that person is not filing or is filing only for a refund.
findings.irs_text: "Even if a child meets the conditions to be the qualifying child of more than one person" and "If you and any other person can claim the child as a qualifying child" (i1040gi 2025, p. 21); compare "Check 'No' if the other person isn't required to file, and isn't filing" (p. 41, Step 3, question 6).
findings.why: A filer could read "meet the conditions" as covering only the listed relationship, age, joint-return, residency and support tests, and answer YES. A filer could also read it as requiring someone who can actually claim the child, by analogy to the non-filer carve-out on p. 41, and answer NO.

question: Were you (or your spouse, if filing jointly) covered in 2025 by two or more dependent care plans that allow different maximum amounts to be excluded?

findings.situation: A filer is covered by two plans that each allow the same maximum below $5,000 (for example, $3,000 each, under two employers), so they truthfully answer NO and the tool enters $3,000 on line 21.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 5, Line 21: "Enter on line 21 the maximum amount that you may exclude for the year under your dependent care plan" and "Don't enter more than the maximum amount allowed under your dependent care plan."
findings.why: The text speaks of one plan's maximum, so it does not settle whether same-maximum plans use the single-plan amount or a combined amount up to the $5,000 limit. This is the same gap the refusal gives for differing maximums, but the question's "different maximum amounts" wording lets this case through to a computed $3,000.

findings.situation: A filer is eligible for or enrolled in two plans with different maximums but received benefits under only one, and could answer YES or NO depending on how they read "covered."
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 5, Line 21: "the maximum amount that you may exclude for the year under your dependent care plan"; Line 12: "Enter the total amount of dependent care benefits you received in 2025."
findings.why: "Covered" could mean merely eligible, enrolled, or actually receiving benefits, while the IRS text ties line 21 to the amount the filer may exclude under their plan. The same facts could therefore lead to either a refusal or a computation using the one plan's maximum.

question: Did you pay in 2025 any qualified expenses for care provided in 2024?

findings.situation: A filer paid in 2025 for care provided in 2024 but already claimed the 2024 credit on the maximum amount of qualified expenses, so there is no additional credit to carry to line 9b.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Did you pay in 2025 any qualified expenses for care provided in 2024?" i2441 (2025) p. 4, Line 9b: "If you had qualified expenses for 2024 that you didn't pay until 2025 and you didn't claim a credit on the maximum amount of qualified expenses for 2024, you may be able to increase the amount of the credit you can take in 2025."
findings.why: The question asks only about the payment, so this filer must answer YES and is refused. The instructions condition the increase on not having claimed the 2024 maximum, so the tool's zero on line 9b appears correct for this filer, although Form 2441 line 9b still routes anyone who paid 2024 expenses in 2025 through Worksheet A, which is not in the supplied text.

question: In 2025, were you (or your spouse, if filing jointly) a full-time student at a school for some part of each of 5 calendar months, or physically or mentally not able to care for yourself at any time? (This includes paying for the care of your spouse who was not able to care for themselves.)

findings.situation: An unmarried filer (single or head of household) who was a full-time student or unable to care for themselves must answer YES and is refused, even though deemed income appears to be available only on a joint return, so the tool's actual earned income would be correct.
findings.irs_text: p503 (2025) p. 11: 'These rules also apply if you are a student or not able to care for yourself and are filing a joint return.' Compare i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'These rules for a spouse who was a student or disabled also apply to you if you were a student or disabled.'
findings.why: The question asks 'were you ... a full-time student ... or physically or mentally not able to care for yourself' without regard to filing status. Pub. 503 limits the filer's own deemed income to joint returns, although i2441 p. 4 states no such limit, so this finding depends on following Pub. 503.

findings.situation: A filer who was a student or unable to care for themselves, and whose actual earned income met or exceeded the $250 or $500 floor in every such month, must answer YES although deemed income would not change lines 4 or 18.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'If you also worked during that month, enter the higher of $250 (or $500) or your actual earned income for that month.'
findings.why: The question asks only about status ('were you ... a full-time student ... or ... not able to care for yourself'), not whether the floor raises income in any month. Where actual earnings are the higher figure every month, the tool's sum of actual earned income is the correct result.

findings.situation: A filer enrolled full-time for 5 or more months only in a correspondence school, an internet-only school, or an on-the-job training course can truthfully answer YES and is refused, although that enrollment does not qualify for deemed income.

question: Elect an alternative allocation of Form 4952 line 4g to qualified dividends instead of capital gains first?

findings.situation: A filer has deductible investment expenses other than interest, such as depreciation or depletion on investment assets or an allowed expense reported on a Schedule K-1, and uses the default allocation or makes no line 4g election, so answers NO.
findings.irs_text: f4952 (2025) p. 4, Line 5: 'Investment expenses are your allowed deductions, other than interest expense, directly connected with the production of investment income. For example, depreciation or depletion allowed on assets that produce investment income is an investment expense.'
findings.why: The question asks only about how line 4g is allocated, so it does not prompt a YES for these expenses. The tool sets line 5 to zero, which overstates net investment income on line 6 and can overstate the deduction on line 8.

findings.situation: A filer whose interest and non-qualified ordinary dividends exceed investment interest, with no carryover and no election, has other deductible investment expenses and truthfully answers NO.
findings.irs_text: f4952 (2025) p. 3, Who Must File: 'You don't have to file Form 4952 if all of the following apply... You don't have any other deductible investment expenses.'
findings.why: The question does not ask about other investment expenses, and the tool treats them as zero. It can therefore treat the filing exception as met and conclude that Form 4952 is not required when the IRS text requires it.

findings.situation: A filer makes an ordinary line 4g election of qualified dividends, either with no net capital gain on line 4e or with the intent to include dividends in investment income, without entering 'Elec.' next to line 4e.
findings.irs_text: f4952 (2025) p. 3, Line 4g: 'you can elect to include part or all of these amounts in investment income'; p. 4, Note: 'you can treat less of the amount on line 4e as attributable to line 4g and more to line 4b... enter on the dotted line next to line 4e "Elec."'
findings.why: 'Elect an alternative allocation of Form 4952 line 4g to qualified dividends' could be read as asking about any election of qualified dividends on line 4g, which would draw a YES on a default-allocation case. It never identifies the specific 'Elec.' entry next to line 4e that the IRS text describes.

findings.situation: A filer wants to treat only part of the line 4g amount as coming from qualified dividends rather than capital gain, keeping some of line 4e attributed to line 4g.
findings.irs_text: f4952 (2025) p. 4, Note: 'you can treat less of the amount on line 4e as attributable to line 4g and more to line 4b... (don't enter less than the excess of line 4g over line 4b)'
findings.why: 'To qualified dividends instead of capital gains first' can be read as describing only a full switch to a dividends-first ordering. A filer making a partial shift, which the tool does not compute, could therefore answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer has no carryover but does have other deductible investment expenses, such as depreciation or depletion on investment assets or K-1 investment expenses, so they answer NO and line 5 is computed as zero.

findings.situation: A filer had disallowed investment interest in an earlier year that was fully used by 2024, so their 2024 Form 4952 line 7 is zero, but they may still answer YES because they once had a carryover.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 1, line 2: "Disallowed investment interest expense from 2024 Form 4952, line 7"; p. 3: "You don't have any carryover of disallowed investment interest expense from 2024."

question: Any interest expense attributable to royalties, a business, passive activities, tax-exempt income or at-risk limitations; any deductible investment expense other than interest (for example depreciation or depletion on assets that produce investment income, or investment expenses on a Schedule K-1); or any other investment income or expense beyond interest, dividends and securities sales?

findings.why: The helper computes only a default-allocation election by carrying over the line 4g amount, and it does not produce the 'Elec.' entry or the smaller line 4e amount used to figure tax. findings.situation: A filer has passive rental mortgage interest, ordinary business loan interest or interest tied to tax-exempt income, none of which is investment interest, and otherwise has only a supported securities-margin situation.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Any interest expense attributable to royalties, a business, passive activities, tax-exempt income..." IRS: "Investment interest expense doesn't include... Interest expense that is properly allocable to a passive activity... Interest expense related to tax-exempt interest income under section 265." (f4952 2025, p. 3, line 1)
findings.why: The wording says 'any interest expense' rather than investment interest, so these filers must answer YES. findings.situation: A filer has mutual fund capital gain distributions or a capital loss carryover and no other unusual items, and must decide whether these go beyond 'interest, dividends and securities sales'.
findings.irs_text: "When figuring this amount, include capital gain distributions from mutual funds and capital loss carryovers." (f4952 2025, p. 3, line 4d)
findings.why: A capital gain distribution can be read as a dividend or as other income because no security was sold, and a carryover can be read as part of securities sales or as a separate item. Filers in the same situation could therefore truthfully answer differently.

findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 3: 'The numerator is the amount you paid and the denominator is the total amount paid by you and all other occupants.'
findings.why: The question turns on co-occupancy alone, and its parenthetical 'whether or not the other occupant files Form 5695' reinforces that breadth. If the other occupant paid nothing, the fraction leaves the ordinary limits unchanged, so the refusal is unnecessary.

findings.situation: Joint occupants each paid for energy items, but their aggregate credit is within every applicable limit, so the question requires YES even though the tool's line 30 is correct on the filer's own amounts.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 3: 'If the aggregate credit that would be allowed to all occupants for any item of property exceeds the credit limit below, then you must figure your allocable share of the credit from each property.'
findings.why: The IRS requires allocation only when an aggregate limit is exceeded, while the question refuses every joint occupant 'whether you paid for the same items or for different ones.' Below the limits, the filer enters the amounts paid and the normal computation applies.

findings.why: Section B property need not be at the main home, but 'the home' could be read as the main home only. A filer reading it that way could answer NO despite needing allocation for property at the shared home.

findings.situation: A filer shared the home only before 2025, or only for part of 2025 before or after the relevant property was paid for or installed, and the question does not say when the joint occupancy must have occurred.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 3: 'If you occupied your home jointly with someone, each occupant must complete their own Form 5695.' i5695 (2025) p. 1: 'A home is where you lived in 2025.'
findings.why: 'Did you occupy' has no time frame, so it could cover any past co-occupancy, any time in 2025, or only the time the property was paid for or installed. Filers in the same situation could therefore truthfully give different answers.

findings.why: The question's examples are all current-year sales or gains, so a filer with only a carryforward from an earlier year could read "disposition adjustment" as not applying.

findings.situation: A filer whose only potentially relevant item is an early withdrawal penalty on Schedule 1, line 18 could answer YES because it is a deductible expense tied to interest income, although the tool computes it on line 10.
findings.irs_text: Question: "a deductible investment expense other than investment interest or state and local tax". IRS: "Early withdrawal penalty (Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 18) is reported on Form 8960, line 10." (i8960 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The question carves out only investment interest and state and local tax, not this penalty, and the penalty is also a line 10 modification that could fit "another net investment income adjustment". The filer could be refused for an item the tool handles.

findings.situation: A beneficiary with a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), box 14, code H adjustment may not know whether an estate or trust distribution counts as "pass-through income", though it affects lines 7 and 13.
findings.irs_text: "Enter the amount from box 14, code H, of Schedule K-1 (Form 1041)" and "enter it on Form 8960, line 7, and increase your MAGI on Form 8960, line 13" (i8960 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: "Pass-through income" can be read to include estates and trusts or to mean only partnerships and S corporations. Estate and trust distributions are not named anywhere in the question.

findings.situation: A filer who owns a CFC or PFIC only indirectly could read "a CFC or PFIC holding" as limited to shares held directly and answer NO, although line 13 may need an adjustment.
findings.irs_text: "If you own, directly or indirectly, stock in a CFC or PFIC" (i8960 2025, p. 22)
findings.why: The IRS text expressly reaches indirect ownership, while "holding" does not say whether it does. The tool would then use AGI as MAGI without the required modification.

findings.situation: A filer who receives pension or other annuity payments from a qualified plan could answer YES to "any annuity" even if the payments are excluded from NII as qualified plan distributions, leaving line 3 correctly at zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Any annuity, rental, royalty, business or pass-through income". IRS: "Annuities (see instructions)" (f8960 2025, line 3); a qualified plan distribution "within the meaning of section 1411(c)(5)" "isn't included in NII" (i8960 2025, p. 9, stated for NUA)
findings.why: "Any annuity" can be read as all annuity payments or only those that count as NII. The Line 3 instructions are not in the supplied text, and the p. 9 language addresses NUA specifically, so this exclusion cannot be fully confirmed here.

question: Did any Marketplace policy, including one whose Form 1095-A went only to someone else, cover someone in your tax family and also someone who is not in it (for example a former spouse, a child someone else claims, or a child you claim whom someone else enrolled), or were you divorced or legally separated during 2025 while enrolled in a policy with your former spouse?

findings.situation: A policy covered the filer's tax family and someone in another tax family, but each family received its own Form 1095-A listing only its own members, so no allocation is needed and the tool computes the filer's lines correctly from their own form.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Did any Marketplace policy, including one whose Form 1095-A went only to someone else, cover someone in your tax family and also someone who is not in it". i8962 (2025) p. 12: allocation is needed if "1. The policy covered at least one individual in your tax family and at least one individual in another tax family; and 2. Either: a. You received a Form 1095-A for the policy that does not accurately represent the members of your tax family who were enrolled in the policy ... or b. The other tax family received a Form 1095-A for the policy that includes a member of your tax family." and "If both (1) and (2) above apply, check 'Yes.'"
findings.why: The question tests only condition 1 and ignores condition 2, so this filer must answer YES even though line 9 is No. The tool then refuses lines it would have computed correctly.

findings.situation: A filer shared a policy with a spouse for part of 2025, the coverage ended, and the couple divorced later in 2025, so the filer was no longer enrolled with the spouse on the divorce date.
findings.irs_text: Question: "were you divorced or legally separated during 2025 while enrolled in a policy with your former spouse?". i8962 (2025) p. 12: "One qualified health plan covers Bret, his spouse Paulette, and their daughter Sophia from January through August ... Bret and Paulette divorce on December 10 ... Bret and Paulette must allocate the amounts from Form 1095-A". i8962 (2025) p. 13, Table 3, Step 1: "For 1 or more months of marriage, the policy covered at least one individual in your tax family AND at least one individual in your former spouse's tax family".
findings.why: "While enrolled" can mean enrolled on the divorce date, which gives NO here, or enrolled at any time in the divorce year, which gives YES as the IRS text requires. The first clause's "former spouse" example may not resolve this, because the person was still a spouse during the coverage months and a filer could read that clause as not reaching them.

question: Does any of these apply: someone enrolled was not lawfully present in the United States; you or a family member were offered or covered by a qualified small employer HRA (QSEHRA, W-2 box 12 code FF) or an individual coverage HRA for 2025; any part of a month's premium was not paid by the due date of your return, not including extensions (or, for coverage you enrolled in retroactively after a successful eligibility appeal, by the 120th day after the appeals decision), or a Form 1095-A shows zero in column A for a month whose premium you paid; or advance payments were made for someone who is in no one's tax family?

findings.situation: A lawfully present alien with household income below 100% of the federal poverty line, who was ineligible for Medicaid because of immigration status, truthfully answers NO, and the tool sets line 24 to zero unless the Marketplace estimate exception applies.
findings.irs_text: i8962 (2025) p. 9: "Alien lawfully present in the United States. Certain aliens with household income below 100% of the federal poverty line are not eligible for Medicaid because of their immigration status. You may qualify for the PTC..."
findings.why: The applicable-taxpayer helper names only line 5 at least 100 or the Marketplace estimate exception, so this second exception is dropped. The question asks only about people not lawfully present, so it does not catch this lawfully present filer.

findings.situation: An enrolled member of the tax family was eligible for other minimum essential coverage, such as CHIP, Medicaid or affordable employer coverage, for some or all of the year, so the filer truthfully answers NO and line 24 may include PTC for coverage that does not qualify.
findings.irs_text: i8962 (2025) p. 6: "Because Kim and Chris were eligible for CHIP, which is MEC, Tom and Nicole are not eligible for the PTC for coverage of Kim and Chris"; p. 4: "Your coverage family includes only individuals in your tax family who are enrolled in a qualified health plan and are not eligible for MEC"
findings.why: The only employer arrangements the question mentions are QSEHRAs and individual coverage HRAs, and it does not ask about any other MEC eligibility. The computation shown has no visible MEC adjustment, and no listed refusal covers this unless the tool handles it through its column inputs or a separate screen.

findings.situation: A filer whom someone else can claim as a dependent, but who files and enters Form 1095-A amounts, truthfully answers NO, and the tool can allow PTC if line 5 is at least 100.
findings.irs_text: i8962 (2025) p. 3: "You can take the PTC for 2025 if you meet the conditions under (1), (2), and (3) below...2. No one can claim you as a dependent for the year."
findings.why: The question does not ask about dependent status, and the applicable-taxpayer helper as described tests only the income conditions. No listed refusal covers this unless a separate screen does.

findings.situation: A filer was offered a QSEHRA but was not covered by it, so the question requires YES even though the instructions quoted here attach QSEHRA consequences only to coverage.
findings.irs_text: Question: "you or a family member were offered or covered by a qualified small employer HRA"; i8962 (2025) p. 1: "If you were covered under a QSEHRA, your employer should have reported the annual permitted benefit in box 12 of your Form W-2 with code FF."
findings.why: The word offered is needed for an individual coverage HRA that was declined, because p. 3 makes PTC depend on its affordability. The supplied text states no comparable rule for a QSEHRA that was offered but did not cover the person, so the tool would refuse a case it can compute.

findings.situation: A relative outside the tax family, or a tax-family member with no Marketplace coverage, was offered or covered by an HRA, so the question requires YES even though the filer's PTC for other enrollees is unaffected.
findings.irs_text: Question: "you or a family member were offered or covered"; i8962 (2025) p. 3: "if another member of your tax family was covered under an individual coverage HRA for 2025, you are not allowed a PTC for the family member's 2025 Marketplace health insurance."
findings.why: The IRS rule removes PTC for the Marketplace insurance of the tax-family member concerned. The question's undefined family member reaches anyone related to the filer, whether or not that person is in the tax family or enrolled in a Marketplace plan.

findings.situation: A filer may be unsure whether family member means a tax-family member, a member of the household, or any relative when answering the HRA part of the question.
findings.irs_text: i8962 (2025) p. 3: "For purposes of the PTC, your tax family consists of the following individuals."
findings.why: The question uses the undefined term family member, while the IRS rule uses the defined term tax family. Filers with relatives outside the tax family could reasonably answer either way.

question: Does this group need an appraisal or other special treatment: a deduction over $5,000 (before any income limit), or property worth more than $5,000, for one item or for similar items (items of the same general category or type, such as coin collections, paintings, books, clothing, jewelry, nonpublicly traded stock, land or buildings) given to all donees together (other than publicly traded securities), a noncash contribution reaching you through a Schedule K-1, vehicles, pass-through entity interests, intellectual property, inventory, conservation or partial interests, property with restrictions on its use, or a clothing or household item over $500 not in good used condition?

findings.situation: A filer gives over $5,000 of stock that trades publicly, such as on an over-the-counter market, but is not regularly traded or has no published quotations, and answers NO because of the publicly traded securities exception.
findings.irs_text: i8283 p. 3, Section A: 'Securities regularly traded in national or regional over-the-counter markets for which published quotations are available'; 'Section B. Include in Section B only items (or groups of similar items) for which you claimed a deduction of more than $5,000.'
findings.why: The undefined phrase 'publicly traded securities' is broader than the listed Section A criteria, so a truthful filer could answer NO. The tool would then compute a gift that may belong in Section B and require a qualified appraisal.

findings.situation: A filer gives a partial interest or restricted-use property with a deduction over $500 but not over $5,000, which must answer YES because the question sets no dollar threshold for these items.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'conservation or partial interests, property with restrictions on its use'. i8283 p. 3: 'You must also file Form 8283, Section B, if conditions were placed on the use of the property or you gave less than an entire interest in a property and the contribution was for more than $5,000.'
findings.why: The Section B rule for these gifts applies only above $5,000, and Section A otherwise covers items with a deduction of $5,000 or less. The question nevertheless refuses them at any amount, even though the tool could enter the deduction amount.

findings.situation: A filer gives a vehicle with a gross-proceeds deduction and a contemporaneous written acknowledgment, intellectual property, or inventory, all of which must answer YES even though these items are reportable in Section A.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'vehicles, ... intellectual property, inventory'. i8283 p. 3, Section A: 'The following items even if the claimed value was more than $5,000 per item', including 'A vehicle ... if your deduction for the vehicle is limited to the gross proceeds from its sale and you obtained a contemporaneous written acknowledgment, f. Intellectual property (as defined later), or g. Inventory'.
findings.why: These items stay in Section A at any value, and the computed line takes a deduction already figured after required reductions. The question sends them to refusal without regard to that treatment.

findings.situation: A filer gives over $5,000 of nonpublic securities that meet the regulation's special Section A rule, which must answer YES because the question excepts only publicly traded securities.
findings.irs_text: i8283 p. 3, Section A: 'Certain other securities even though the securities do not meet any of the criteria described in paragraphs 2.a through 2.c above (for more information, see Regulations section 1.170A-13(c)(7)(xi)(B))'.
findings.why: These securities are reportable in Section A even above $5,000, but they are not publicly traded under the listed criteria. The question's exception therefore does not reach them.

findings.situation: A filer gives over $5,000 of mutual fund shares and could reasonably read 'publicly traded securities' either to include or to exclude them.
findings.irs_text: i8283 p. 3, Section A: 'Securities that are shares of a mutual fund for which quotations are published on a daily basis in a newspaper of general circulation throughout the United States'.
findings.why: Mutual fund shares are often bought from and redeemed through the fund rather than traded on a market, so a filer could think the exception does not apply. The IRS text places qualifying shares in Section A, but the question does not say so.

question: Was your earned income credit for any year after 1996, or your child tax credit, additional child tax credit or credit for other dependents for any year after 2015, reduced or disallowed for any reason other than a math or clerical error, or are you in a 2- or 10-year period during which you can't take one of these credits because an earlier claim was found to be reckless, intentional or fraudulent?

findings.situation: A filer's EIC was disallowed in an earlier year, but the filer later filed Form 8862, the EIC was allowed for that year, and it has not been reduced or disallowed again, so the filer must answer YES although no Form 8862 is needed for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "But don’t file Form 8862 if either of the following applies. • You filed Form 8862 for another year, the EIC was allowed for that year, and your EIC hasn’t been reduced or disallowed again for any reason other than a math or clerical error."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the credit "for any year after 1996" was "reduced or disallowed" and has no carve-out for a later successful recertification. The tool's computation would be correct for this filer because the IRS text requires no Form 8862.

findings.situation: A filer is taking the EIC without a qualifying child, and the only reason an earlier EIC was reduced or disallowed was that a child on Schedule EIC was found not to be a qualifying child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "You are taking the EIC without a qualifying child and the only reason your EIC was reduced or disallowed in the other year was because it was determined that a child listed on Schedule EIC wasn’t your qualifying child."
findings.why: The question's phrase "reduced or disallowed for any reason other than a math or clerical error" requires YES, but the IRS text says not to file Form 8862 here. The tool would refuse a credit it can compute correctly.

findings.situation: A filer's CTC, ACTC or ODC was denied or reduced in an earlier year, but the filer filed Form 8862 for 2024 and the credit was allowed for that year, or another exception applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 39: "Don’t file Form 8862 if you filed Form 8862 for 2024, and the child tax credit, additional child tax credit, or credit for other dependents was allowed for that year." i1040s8812 p. 2: "you must attach Form 8862 to your tax return to claim the CTC, ACTC, or ODC unless an exception applies."
findings.why: The question has no exception for an earlier recertification, so this filer must answer YES. The IRS text does not require Form 8862 for this filer, so the tool's computation would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer has a past reduction, disallowance or ban affecting only one credit family, such as the EIC, and claims only the other family, such as the CTC, yet the single answer refuses both lines.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "You must file Form 8862 if your EIC for a year after 1996 was reduced or disallowed" and "10 years after the most recent tax year for which there was a final determination that your EIC claim was due to fraud." i1040s8812 p. 2: "If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced ... you must attach Form 8862 ... to claim the CTC, ACTC, or ODC" and "you will not be allowed to claim any of these credits for 10 years."
findings.why: The question joins both families with "or" and refers to "one of these credits," so a history with either family produces YES and refuses both lines. The quoted IRS text ties each Form 8862 requirement and ban to its own credit family, so the unaffected line would compute correctly.

findings.situation: A filer's earlier CTC or ODC was limited only by the income phase-out or by tax liability, and the IRS never denied or adjusted the claim.
findings.irs_text: i1040s8812 p. 2: "The maximum credit amount of your CTC and ODC may be reduced if either (1) or (2) applies." Compare: "If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced for any reason other than a math or clerical error, you must attach Form 8862."
findings.why: The question's "reduced ... for any reason" does not say the reduction must be an IRS action on a claim, and the instructions also use "reduced" for the ordinary limits. A filer could reasonably answer YES because of a phase-out or tax limit, or NO because the IRS did not change the claim.

question: Do any wage statements report railroad retirement compensation or taxes (W-2 box 14), or did you file Form CT-2 as an employee representative?

findings.situation: A filer with no railroad compensation has uncollected Medicare tax on tips (W-2 box 12, code B) or on group-term life insurance for former employees (code N), so they truthfully answer NO, and the tool totals box 6 only.
findings.irs_text: i8959 p. 4, Line 19: "Also include any uncollected Medicare tax on tips from Form W-2, box 12, code B, and any uncollected Medicare tax on the taxable cost of group-term life insurance over $50,000 (for former employees) from Form W-2, box 12, code N."
findings.why: The question asks only about railroad compensation or taxes and Form CT-2, so it never reaches these non-RRTA amounts. The computed person.medicare6 line omits them, which understates Form 8959 line 19.

findings.situation: A filer whose wage statement is Form 499R-2/W-2PR has Medicare wages and tax withheld in boxes 22 and 23, so they truthfully answer NO, and the tool reads only boxes 5 and 6.
findings.irs_text: i8959 p. 1: "for Form 499R-2/W-2PR, Medicare wages and tips are reported in box 22 and Medicare tax withheld is reported in box 23."
findings.why: The question does not address Puerto Rico wage statements. If boxes 5 and 6 are absent from that form, person.medicare5 and person.medicare6 can treat the amounts that belong on Form 8959 lines 1 and 19 as zero.

findings.situation: A filer with one railroad employer, no other wages, and RRTA compensation of $200,000 or less must answer YES, although the computed lines would correctly give no excess social security credit and no wage-based Form 8959 amounts.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 11: "had more than one employer for 2025 and total wages of more than $176,100"; i8959 p. 1: "Your RRTA compensation on any single Form W-2 (box 14) is greater than $200,000."
findings.why: "Do any wage statements report railroad retirement compensation or taxes" is triggered by any RRTA amount. This filer has no Line 11 credit and no Additional Medicare Tax on RRTA compensation, and iw2w3 p. 13 says boxes 3 through 7 are not used for railroad amounts, so the zeros would be correct.

findings.situation: A railroad employee's W-2 box 14 may show labels such as "Tier 1 tax," "Tier 2 tax," or "Medicare tax" without the word "railroad," so the filer may not recognize them as railroad retirement taxes.
findings.irs_text: iw2w3 p. 12: "Label them 'RRTA compensation,' 'Tier 1 tax,' 'Tier 2 tax,' 'Medicare tax,' and 'Additional Medicare Tax.'"
findings.why: The question does not list these labels. A filer could read "Medicare tax" or "Tier 1 tax" in box 14 as something other than railroad retirement tax and answer NO.

findings.situation: "Did you file Form CT-2" states no tax year, so a representative who filed it only for another year, or who has not yet filed for 2025, could reasonably answer either way.
findings.irs_text: i8959 p. 4, Line 14: "include the total of the compensation amounts from line 2 of all Forms CT-2 filed for 2025"
findings.why: The IRS text concerns Forms CT-2 filed for 2025, but the question's past-tense wording has no year. A filer could count a form filed for a different year or leave out a 2025 form still to be filed.

question: As the designated beneficiary of an ABLE account, did you contribute to it for 2025, or did you receive any distribution from an ABLE account after 2022 and before the due date of your 2025 return (including extensions)?

findings.situation: A designated beneficiary whose only ABLE activity was a distribution not taxable because it was rolled over or moved by trustee-to-trustee transfer must answer YES, although the distribution is excluded from line 4 and the tool's zero is correct.
findings.irs_text: f8880 (2025) p. 2, Line 4: "Don't include any of the following. • Distributions not taxable as the result of a rollover or a trustee-to-trustee transfer."
findings.why: The question asks about "any distribution from an ABLE account" without the Line 4 exclusions. This filer is refused even though the excluded amount does not change the computed lines.

findings.situation: A designated beneficiary whose only ABLE distribution was a return of excess contributions and allocable income must answer YES, although that distribution is excluded from line 4 and the tool's zero is correct.
findings.irs_text: f8880 (2025) p. 2, Line 4: "Don't include any of the following. ... • Distributions of excess contributions or deferrals (and income allocable to such contributions or deferrals)."
findings.why: "Any distribution" has no carve-out for returned excess contributions. The filer must answer YES even though Line 4 excludes the amount.

findings.situation: A designated beneficiary whose only 2025 ABLE contribution was a rollover contribution would truthfully answer YES if they treat it as contributing, although line 1 excludes it and the tool's zero is correct.
findings.irs_text: f8880 (2025) p. 1, line 1: "Traditional and Roth IRA contributions, and ABLE account contributions by the designated beneficiary for 2025. Do not include rollover contributions"

question: Does this distribution involve any of these: a disability pension received before minimum retirement age, or a pension partly excludable because you were disabled as a result of a terrorist attack; a corrective distribution of excess deferrals or contributions; a qualified charitable distribution or HSA funding distribution; nondeductible contributions to any traditional IRA; a conversion or recharacterization (Form 8606); a 2024 or 2025 IRA contribution returned to you, or excess contributions for an earlier year returned to you in 2025; a rollover to a Roth IRA or designated Roth account; a lump-sum distribution you may report on Form 4972; a nonqualified annuity; the retired public safety officer premium exclusion; a death benefit exclusion; a military disability pension; an annuity you receive as the beneficiary of an employee who died, or that is shared among more than one beneficiary; a rollover of property other than cash, or of a distribution under a qualified domestic relations order; a plan loan offset; a Form RRB-1099-R; U.S. Civil Service retirement benefits under the alternative annuity option (Pub. 721); or a pension or annuity in which you have after-tax cost whose annuity starting date was before November 19, 1996, or for which the Simplified Method does not apply (the General Rule)?

findings.situation: A filer receives a Roth IRA distribution that is not code Q and not a code T distribution meeting the pre-2021 contribution test, such as a nonqualified code J distribution, with no conversion or recharacterization involved.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "You received a distribution from a Roth IRA. But if either (a) or (b) below applies, enter -0- on line 4b; you don't have to see Form 8606 or its instructions."
findings.why: The question's Form 8606 items cover traditional IRA nondeductible contributions, conversions, recharacterizations and returned contributions, but not an ordinary nonqualified Roth IRA distribution, so the filer can truthfully answer NO. The tool then uses the part not rolled over as the taxable amount and skips the Form 8606 figuring the instructions require.

findings.situation: A filer's IRA distribution is separate from a 2025 conversion, recharacterization or returned contribution, or the filer's nondeductible contributions were made in earlier years to a different traditional IRA.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "You received a distribution from an IRA (other than a Roth IRA) and you made nondeductible contributions to any of your traditional IRAs for 2025 or an earlier year"; "You converted part or all of a traditional IRA or traditional SIMPLE IRA to a Roth IRA in 2025."
findings.why: Exception 2 turns on the filer's IRA history, but the question asks whether "this distribution" involves these items, so a filer could reasonably answer NO for a separate distribution. The broad wording could also lead a filer to answer YES for a qualified Roth IRA or pension distribution merely because they have nondeductible traditional IRA contributions.

findings.situation: A filer takes a nonperiodic or lump-sum distribution from an employer plan with after-tax contributions in box 5, and may have rolled over part of it.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 30, Rollovers: "From this amount, subtract any contributions (usually shown in box 5) that were taxable to you when made. From that result, subtract the amount of the rollover."
findings.why: The question reaches after-tax cost only for "a pension or annuity" where the Simplified Method does not apply, and its parenthetical "(the General Rule)" suggests annuity payments rather than a one-time distribution. A filer could reasonably answer either way, although the tool's computation addresses after-tax cost only through the Simplified Method for an annuity.

question: Does any of these apply to alimony you received or paid: payments under more than one divorce or separation agreement, or paid to more than one person; a recapture of alimony (payments that decreased or ended during the first 3 calendar years, Pub. 504 Worksheet 1); or payments of which part is not alimony: child support (including payments that fell short of the total of child support and alimony required, and an amount the instrument reduces on a contingency relating to a child, such as reaching a certain age, or at a time associated with one), or payments for a home either of you owns (mortgage, real estate taxes, insurance, repairs; Pub. 504 Table 4)?

findings.situation: A payer's fixed annual payment is partly not alimony because that part must continue, or be replaced by a substitute payment, after the recipient's death, as when a $10,000 trust payment after death makes $10,000 of a $30,000 annual payment not alimony.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 15: 'If any part of payments you make must continue to be made for any period after your spouse's death, that part of your payments isn't alimony'; 'Of each of the $30,000 annual payments, $10,000 isn't alimony.'
findings.why: The question's list of non-alimony parts names only child support and home payments, so this filer truthfully answers NO. The tool then carries the $30,000 a filer would naturally enter, with no prompt to reduce it.

findings.situation: Amounts under an instrument include a noncash property settlement or the recipient's own share of community income.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 13: 'Alimony doesn't include: Child support, Noncash property settlements, Payments that are your spouse's part of community income'
findings.why: The colon after 'payments of which part is not alimony' introduces what reads as a closed list that omits these two categories. A filer can answer NO, and the tool may treat these amounts as alimony.

findings.situation: A pre-2019 agreement was changed after 2018 to expressly provide that the alimony is not included in the recipient's income or deductible by the payer, possibly affecting only part of 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 89, Line 2a: 'unless that agreement was changed after December 31, 2018, to expressly provide that alimony received isn't included in your income'; p504 p. 16, Example 2: 'The alimony payments made in June 2025 through December 2025 are neither includible in the recipient's income nor deductible from the payer's income.'
findings.why: The question does not ask about modified agreements, and the helper label as quoted covers any agreement entered into on or before December 31, 2018. This filer answers NO, and the tool can include or deduct amounts that the modification excludes.

findings.situation: A payer makes mortgage or real estate tax payments on a home owned only by the recipient, and those payments fully qualify as alimony.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'payments for a home either of you owns (mortgage, real estate taxes, insurance, repairs; Pub. 504 Table 4)'. p504 p. 13, Example 2: 'you must pay the real estate taxes and mortgage payments on a home owned by your spouse. If they otherwise qualify, you can deduct the payments as alimony'
findings.why: The wording lists a home owned by either person as a non-alimony item, so this filer answers YES. Yet the full amount is alimony and the tool computes it correctly.

findings.situation: Alimony decreased or ended during the first 3 calendar years, but no recapture applies for 2025 because the decrease is too small, is excluded (such as death or remarriage), or does not produce a third-year recapture in 2025.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'a recapture of alimony (payments that decreased or ended during the first 3 calendar years, Pub. 504 Worksheet 1)'. p504 p. 16: 'You are subject to the recapture rule in the third year if the alimony you pay in the third year decreases by more than $15,000 from the second year or the alimony you pay in the second and third years decreases significantly'; 'Payments that decrease because of the death of either spouse or the remarriage'
findings.why: The parenthetical presents any decrease or ending as a recapture, so a filer with no 2025 recapture can answer YES. The tool computes that filer's ordinary alimony correctly.

findings.situation: The listed facts, such as child support or a second agreement, involve an instrument executed after 2018, whose payments are outside the helper amounts.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'Does any of these apply to alimony you received or paid'. p504 p. 12: 'Amounts paid as alimony or separate maintenance payments under a divorce or separation instrument executed after 2018 won't be deductible by the payer. Such amounts also won't be includible in the income of the recipient.'
findings.why: The question is not limited to pre-2019 agreements, so this filer answers YES. The post-2018 payments have no effect on these lines, and the tool correctly leaves them out because its helpers cover only agreements entered into on or before December 31, 2018.

findings.situation: An instrument separately fixes child support and alimony, the filer pays the full total, and only the alimony amount is entered.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'payments of which part is not alimony: child support'. p504 p. 13: 'If you pay the full amount of $4,200 ($2,400 + $1,800) during the year, you can deduct $1,800 as alimony and your former spouse must report $1,800 as alimony received'
findings.why: A filer can read this arrangement as child support within the payments and answer YES. Entering the separately stated $1,800 would nonetheless compute correctly, and the question's specific shortfall and contingency examples imply no such calculation is needed here.

findings.situation: A payer pays expenses for a home owned jointly by both spouses or former spouses.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 13: 'If your divorce or separation instrument states that you must pay expenses for a home owned by you and your spouse or former spouse, some of your payments may be alimony. See Table 4.'
findings.why: 'A home either of you owns' can mean a home owned by one person or can include one owned by both. The Table 4 citation points toward joint ownership, but a filer may not be able to tell that from the question.

findings.situation: An alimony reduction occurs near, but not clearly within, the periods presumed to be associated with a child-related contingency.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'at a time associated with one'. p504 pp. 15-16: 'not more than 6 months before or after the date the child will reach 18, 21, or local age of majority'; 'In all other situations, reductions in payments aren't treated as clearly associated with the happening of a contingency relating to your child.'
findings.why: The loose phrase 'associated with' omits the IRS test of 'clearly associated' and its specific time windows. A filer could answer either way when a reduction merely falls around a child's milestone.

question: Does any of these apply to a canceled debt: it was canceled in a bankruptcy case or while you were insolvent, or is otherwise excluded from income (Form 982, for example qualified principal residence indebtedness); it was a student loan, was canceled as a gift or inheritance, was a reduction of the price of property you bought from the seller, or was owed to a corporation in which you hold stock; it was a business, rental or farm debt; it was canceled in connection with a foreclosure, repossession or abandonment of property (Form 1099-C box 7, or a Form 1099-A); it includes interest (Form 1099-C box 3) or any other amount (for example an unpaid medical bill) that would have been deductible if you had paid it; you were not personally liable for it (box 5); or you and someone other than your spouse on this return were both liable for it?

findings.situation: A filer sells a personal-use property, such as a second home, in a short sale or gives a deed in lieu, and the lender cancels the rest of a recourse mortgage, with no Form 1099-A or Form 1099-C box 7 entry.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 4: "Sales or Other Dispositions (Such as Foreclosures and Repossessions)"; p525 p. 20: "you're relieved of the mortgage when you dispose of the property... To the extent the mortgage discharge exceeds the FMV of the property, it's income from discharge of indebtedness"
findings.why: The question names only foreclosure, repossession or abandonment, so this filer could truthfully answer NO even though the IRS applies the disposition rules to other dispositions too. The tool would then enter the full canceled amount without testing the discharge against FMV or addressing gain or loss on the disposition.

findings.situation: A filer's Form 1099-C box 3 shows nondeductible interest, such as interest on a personal credit card or personal loan, and the rest of the debt is fully taxable.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 20: "If the interest would not be deductible (such as interest on a personal loan), include in your income the amount from box 2 of Form 1099-C."
findings.why: In "it includes interest (Form 1099-C box 3) or any other amount... that would have been deductible," the deductibility condition may modify interest or only "any other amount." On the first reading this filer answers NO and the tool correctly uses box 2; on the second the filer answers YES and is wrongly refused.

findings.situation: A filer has a canceled nonbusiness student loan that does not qualify for any exception or exclusion, such as a loan from an educational organization canceled because of services performed for that organization.
findings.irs_text: Question: "it was a student loan"; p4681 p. 4: "The cancellation of your loan won't qualify for tax-free treatment if it was made by an educational organization or tax-exempt section 501(c)(3) organization and was canceled because of the services you performed for either organization."
findings.why: The question makes every canceled student loan a YES, whether or not it is excluded. A fully taxable canceled student loan is nonbusiness debt that the tool could correctly enter at its full amount.

findings.situation: A filer who is not personally liable on a nonbusiness debt keeps the collateral and receives an early-payment discount or a loan modification that reduces principal, with no exclusion applying.
findings.irs_text: Question: "you were not personally liable for it (box 5)"; p4681 p. 3: "you don't have ordinary income from the cancellation of debt unless you retain the collateral and either: • The lender offers a discount for the early payment of the debt, or • The lender agrees to a loan modification that results in the reduction of the principal balance of the debt."
findings.why: The question makes all nonrecourse debt a YES, but in this situation the discount or principal reduction is canceled debt that must be included in income. The tool could correctly enter that amount if it is the amount reported.

question: Do you have any income (or loss or exclusion) for Schedule 1, line 8, other than gambling winnings (line 8b), canceled debt (line 8c), income from Form 8889 (line 8f), Alaska Permanent Fund dividends (line 8g), jury duty pay (line 8h), prizes and awards (line 8i), income from an activity not engaged in for profit (line 8j), scholarship and fellowship grants not reported on Form W-2 (line 8r) and the other income asked item by item for line 8z? For example: a net operating loss deduction (8a); the foreign earned income or housing exclusion from Form 2555 (8d); income from Form 8853 (8e); stock options (8k); income from the rental of personal property (8l); Olympic and Paralympic medals or USOC prize money (8m); a section 951(a) or 951A(a) inclusion (8n, 8o); a section 461(l) excess business loss adjustment (8p); taxable distributions from an ABLE account (8q); nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments (8s); a pension or annuity from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan or a nongovernmental section 457 plan (8t); wages earned while incarcerated (8u); or digital assets received as ordinary income not reported elsewhere (8v).

findings.situation: A filer has income from renting personal property in an activity not engaged in for profit, which belongs on line 8j and which the tool computes, but the question's example tells them to answer YES.
findings.irs_text: Question: "income from the rental of personal property (8l)". i1040gi p. 91, Line 8l: "Income from the rental of personal property if you engaged in the rental for profit but were not in the business of renting such property."
findings.why: The example drops the for-profit limit in the line 8l text, so it also describes not-for-profit rentals that the tool handles on line 8j. The question excludes line 8j income but also names this rental income, so a filer following the example is refused unnecessarily.

findings.situation: A filer received nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments that were not included on Form 1040, line 1a or 1d, so the line 8s amount is zero, but the question's example prompts a YES.
findings.irs_text: Question: "nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments (8s)". f1040s1 p. 1, line 8s: "Nontaxable amount of Medicaid waiver payments included on Form 1040, line 1a or 1d"; i1040gi p. 92: "enter the total amount of the nontaxable payments reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1a or 1d".
findings.why: Line 8s only reverses payments included on line 1a or 1d, a limit the example omits. A filer with excluded payments that were never included has nothing to subtract, and the tool's zero is correct, yet the example reads as covering them.

findings.situation: A filer has taxable line 8z income that the tool does not ask about individually, such as an insurance policy dividend exceeding net premiums, and may not know whether it is among the items asked.
findings.irs_text: Question: "the other income asked item by item for line 8z". i1040gi p. 91-92, Line 8z: "Use line 8z to report any taxable income not reported elsewhere on your return or other schedules."
findings.why: The question does not list the supported items or use an unsupported line 8z item as an example, so a filer could read the phrase as excluding all line 8z income and answer NO. If that item is not captured elsewhere, it would be omitted from line 9.

findings.situation: A filer exercised stock options and all the resulting income is already reported as wages on Form 1040, line 1h, leaving nothing for line 8k.
findings.irs_text: Question: "stock options (8k)". i1040gi p. 91, Line 8k: "Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h."
findings.why: The example omits the "not otherwise reported" limit, although the 8v example includes similar wording. A filer could answer YES because they have stock option income, or NO because none of it belongs on line 8k, and YES would cause an unnecessary refusal.
