question: Did you, in 2025 or any earlier year, make contributions to a governmental unemployment compensation program (including amounts withheld from your wages for it; not counting employer-paid tax, paid family leave or disability insurance contributions), or repay in 2025 any unemployment compensation you included in income in an earlier year?

findings.situation: A filer who received no unemployment compensation in 2025 but had state unemployment contributions withheld from wages in 2025 or an earlier year must answer YES, even though line 7 is correctly zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'Did you, in 2025 or any earlier year, make contributions to a governmental unemployment compensation program (including amounts withheld from your wages for it...'; i1040gi (2025) p. 89, line 7 Caution: 'reduce the amount you report on line 7 by those contributions.'
findings.why: The question is not limited to filers who received unemployment compensation in 2025, so it can refuse a filer with no line 7 amount to reduce. The tool's computation yields the correct zero for this filer.

findings.situation: A filer who repaid $3,000 or less in 2025 of unemployment compensation included in income in an earlier year must answer YES, although the line 7 text calls for no adjustment for that repayment.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'or repay in 2025 any unemployment compensation you included in income in an earlier year'; i1040gi (2025) p. 89, line 7: 'If, in 2025, you repaid more than $3,000 of unemployment compensation that you included in gross income in an earlier year, see Repayments in Pub. 525.'
findings.why: The question uses 'any' while the cited text addresses only repayments over $3,000 and does not reduce line 7 for smaller ones. On this text, the tool computes line 7 correctly for a smaller repayment, although the supplied text does not address treatment elsewhere on the return.

findings.situation: A self-employed filer who personally pays contributions for elective coverage under a state unemployment program could read those payments as either the filer's own contributions or excluded employer-paid tax.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 89, line 7 Caution: 'If you made contributions to a governmental unemployment compensation program and you aren't itemizing deductions, reduce the amount you report on line 7 by those contributions.'
findings.why: The exclusion for 'employer-paid tax' does not say how it applies when the filer is both employer and covered worker. A NO answer would make the tool skip the reduction the IRS text requires.

question: Are you required to file Form 6251 or do you have an AMT adjustment requiring its review?

findings.situation: A filer who owes no AMT but has an amount on line 7, 9, 13, 14, 15, 16, or 19 (for example, household employment taxes or uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax) can truthfully answer NO, and computed line 21 omits that amount.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 (2025) p. 2, line 21: "Add lines 4, 7 through 16, 18, and 19. These are your total other taxes"; p. 1, line 9: "Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H"
findings.why: The tool adds only lines 4, 8, 11, 12, and 18, while the question asks only about Form 6251 and AMT adjustments. No listed refusal covers the omitted lines, so line 21 is understated on a NO answer.

findings.situation: A filer who has an AMT adjustment item or must file Form 6251 but owes no AMT on line 2 must answer YES, even though the computed zero on line 2 would be correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are you required to file Form 6251 or do you have an AMT adjustment requiring its review?"; f1040s2 (2025) p. 1, line 2: "Alternative minimum tax. Attach Form 6251"
findings.why: Having an adjustment or a filing requirement does not by itself mean a positive amount belongs on line 2. The question therefore refuses some filers whose lines 2, 3, and 21 the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer with a possible AMT preference or adjustment item cannot tell from the question whether it is one "requiring its review" or whether Form 6251 is required without first working through that form.
findings.irs_text: Question: "do you have an AMT adjustment requiring its review?"; f1040s2 (2025) p. 1, line 2: "Alternative minimum tax. Attach Form 6251"
findings.why: The question gives no test for when an adjustment requires review or when Form 6251 must be filed, and the line text supplies none. Similar filers could reasonably answer differently, and a NO could leave AMT owed treated as zero.

question: Were you a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico in 2025?

findings.situation: A filer with three or more qualifying children who was not a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico in 2025 but had social security or Medicare tax withheld on Puerto Rico Form 499R-2/W-2PR, for example from Puerto Rico wages, truthfully answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040s8812 p. 5, Credit Limit Worksheet B, line 7: "Social security tax withheld from Form(s) W-2, box 4, and Puerto Rico Form(s) 499R-2/W-2PR, box 21" and "Medicare tax withheld from Form(s) W-2, box 6, and Puerto Rico Form(s) 499R-2/W-2PR, box 23"
findings.why: Worksheet line 7 counts Puerto Rico withholding without conditioning it on bona fide residency, but the question asks only about residency, so this filer is not refused. The excerpt does not show the tool's line 7 inputs; if it reads only Form W-2 boxes 4 and 6, clwb_11 and the amount carried to line 27 can be understated.

findings.situation: A bona fide resident of Puerto Rico must answer YES and is refused even when Part II-B or worksheet lines 7 through 10 cannot change the result, such as when line 20 is equal to or more than line 17, worksheet line 5 is equal to or more than line 1, or line 16a or 16b is zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Were you a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico in 2025?" f1040s8812 p. 2: "Yes. If line 20 is equal to or more than line 17, skip Part II-B and enter the amount from line 17 on line 27"; "If zero, stop here; you cannot take the additional child tax credit." i1040s8812 p. 5, line 6: "If you are a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico and line 5 above is less than line 1 above, go to line 7. Otherwise, leave lines 7 through 10 blank, enter -0- on line 11"
findings.why: The IRS text sends a Puerto Rico resident through the special path only when the earned-income amount falls short of the credit limit. In these other cases the computed lines give the correct result (with fewer than three children, line 26 is at least line 20, so line 27 still equals line 17), yet the question refuses them.

findings.situation: A filer who lived in Puerto Rico for only part of 2025, or who moved there or away during the year, could reasonably answer either YES or NO.
findings.irs_text: f1040s8812 p. 2: "If you are a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico, go to line 21"; i1040s8812 p. 5, line 6: "If you are a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico and line 5 above is less than line 1 above, go to line 7"
findings.why: The question's "in 2025" does not say whether part of the year is enough, and the quoted IRS text states no period of residence. A truthful part-year resident could therefore answer NO and receive the non-Puerto Rico computation, or answer YES and be refused.

findings.situation: A filer who lives or works in Puerto Rico may not know whether they meet the legal standard for being a "bona fide resident," and the question gives no definition or test.
findings.irs_text: f1040s8812 p. 2: "If you are a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico, go to line 21"
findings.why: The question repeats the IRS term of art, and neither it nor the quoted IRS text explains the term. A filer could reasonably equate it with simply living in Puerto Rico or read it as a stricter status, leading to different answers on the same facts.

question: Are any charitable deductions reduced by income limits, or carried over from a prior year? Determine under Publication 526 before answering.

findings.situation: A filer paid foreign income tax or generation-skipping tax on income distributions and wants to deduct it as an itemized deduction, but has no limited or carried-over charitable gifts.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "Include on this line income taxes you paid to a foreign country and generation-skipping tax (GST) imposed on certain income distributions."
findings.why: The question asks only about charitable deductions, so this filer truthfully answers NO. The tool then enters zero on line 6 and understates line 17.

findings.situation: A filer paid home mortgage interest not reported on Form 1098, such as interest paid to the person from whom the home was bought, but has no limited or carried-over charitable gifts.

findings.why: Mortgage interest has nothing to do with the charitable wording, so the filer answers NO. The tool then enters zero on line 8b.

findings.situation: A filer has deductible points that were not reported on Form 1098, but has no limited or carried-over charitable gifts.
findings.irs_text: f1040sa (2025) p. 1, line 8c: "Points not reported to you on Form 1098. See instructions for special rules"
findings.why: The charitable wording does not reach points, so the filer answers NO. The tool then enters zero on line 8c.

findings.situation: A filer has a personal casualty or theft loss from a federally declared disaster on Form 4684, line 18, but has no limited or carried-over charitable gifts.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p. 11, Line 15: "Complete and attach Form 4684 to figure the amount of your loss. Only enter the amount from Form 4684, line 18, on line 15."
findings.why: The question does not mention casualty losses, so the filer answers NO. The tool then enters zero on line 15.

findings.situation: A filer has a line 16 deduction other than gambling losses: a casualty or theft loss of income-producing property, federal estate tax on income in respect of a decedent, amortizable bond premium, or an ordinary loss on a contingent payment or inflation-indexed debt instrument.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p. 11, Other Itemized Deductions: "Casualty and theft losses of income-producing property... Federal estate tax on income in respect of a decedent... A deduction for amortizable bond premium... An ordinary loss attributable to a contingent payment debt instrument or an inflation-indexed debt instrument"
findings.why: None of these items is charitable, so the filer answers NO. The tool's line 16 computes only gambling losses and omits them.

findings.situation: A filer has a net qualified disaster loss on Form 4684, line 15, whether itemizing or claiming the increased standard deduction through Schedule A.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p. 11, Line 16: "If you have a net qualified disaster loss on Form 4684, line 15, and you are itemizing your deductions, list the amount... and include with your other miscellaneous deductions on line 16"; "you can claim an increased standard deduction using Schedule A"
findings.why: The charitable wording does not cover a disaster loss, so the filer answers NO. The tool's line 16 omits the loss, and neither of its reporting methods is computed.

findings.situation: A filer has an unused charitable contribution from more than 5 years ago, or an earlier-year carryover that the limits leave with no amount deductible this year.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p. 11, Line 13: "In most cases, you have 5 years to use contributions that were limited in an earlier year... enter the amount of your carryover that you are allowed to deduct this year."
findings.why: "Carried over from a prior year" could mean any leftover prior-year amount or only an amount deductible this year. A filer could answer either way, although a NO with zero on line 13 would be correct when nothing is allowed this year.

findings.situation: A filer gave appreciated property and must reduce the deduction by the ordinary income or capital gain that a sale would have produced, but is not otherwise limited by a percentage of income.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p. 11, Recordkeeping: "The cost or other basis of the property if you must reduce it by any ordinary income or capital gain that would have resulted if the property had been sold at its fair market value"
findings.why: "Reduced by income limits" most naturally means percentage limits, but a filer could also read it to include this reduction based on ordinary income or gain. The filer could therefore answer YES or NO on the same facts.

question: Are you required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR)? Determine under its instructions; this tool does not determine foreign account values or exceptions.

findings.situation: A filer received a Form 1099-INT that includes interest received as a nominee (or accrued interest paid on a bond purchase), has no foreign accounts, and so truthfully answers NO; the tool then puts the gross roster total on line 2 without the required subtraction.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.1: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total interest you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 2." p.2: "follow the rules earlier under Nominees ... identify the amount to be subtracted as 'Accrued Interest.'"
findings.why: Line 2 computes only the sum of interest.amount, but the IRS text requires subtracting nominee, accrued-interest, OID and ABP adjustments. FBAR status has nothing to do with these adjustments, so the screen never catches them.

findings.situation: A filer cashed post-1989 series EE or I bonds and paid qualified higher education expenses, has no foreign accounts, and so answers NO; line 3 is then forced to zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.2, Line 3: "If, during 2025, you cashed series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 and you paid qualified higher education expenses ... you may be able to exclude part or all of the interest on those bonds. See Form 8815"
findings.why: Line 3 is hard-coded to zero, and the FBAR question gives a filer entitled to the Form 8815 exclusion no reason to answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer received a Form 1099-DIV that includes ordinary dividends received as a nominee, has no foreign accounts, and so answers NO; line 6 then takes box 1a gross.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.2, Line 5 Nominees: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total ordinary dividends you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 6."
findings.why: Line 6 copies box 1a with no nominee subtraction, and FBAR status does not bring this situation to light.

findings.situation: A filer who must file an FBAR (foreign accounts above $10,000 in aggregate) but has only ordinary Form 1099-INT/1099-DIV amounts with no adjustments answers YES, and lines 2, 3 and 6 are refused even though the tool would compute them correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are you required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR)?" i1040sb p.3: "A U.S. person that has a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts must file the form if the aggregate value of foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000"
findings.why: The FBAR requirement affects Part III (lines 7a/7b), not the interest and dividend amounts on lines 2, 3 and 6. A YES answer therefore blocks lines whose computation does not depend on it.

question: Are you required to file Form 8938 for specified foreign financial assets?

findings.situation: A filer received a Form 1099-INT that includes interest received as a nominee, has no foreign assets, and so truthfully answers NO; the tool then puts the full interest on line 2 without subtracting the nominee distribution.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total interest you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 2."
findings.why: Line 2 is the line 1 subtotal less nominee amounts, but the tool only adds interest entries. The Form 8938 question has nothing to do with nominee status, so this filer is never screened out.

findings.situation: A filer must subtract accrued interest paid on a bond purchase, an OID adjustment, or an amortizable bond premium adjustment, answers NO because they have no foreign assets, and the tool reports gross interest on line 2.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "follow the rules earlier under Nominees to see how to report the accrued interest. But identify the amount to be subtracted as 'Accrued Interest.'" (similarly "OID Adjustment" and "ABP Adjustment")
findings.why: These subtractions reduce line 2 below the sum of interest entries. The tool does not make them, and a question about Form 8938 does not reach them.

findings.situation: A filer cashed post-1989 series EE or I savings bonds and paid qualified higher education expenses, answers NO because they have no foreign assets, and the tool sets line 3 to zero instead of the Form 8815 exclusion.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Line 3. If, during 2025, you cashed series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 and you paid qualified higher education expenses ... you may be able to exclude part or all of the interest on those bonds. See Form 8815"
findings.why: Line 3 is computed as a fixed zero, but the IRS text calls for a Form 8815 exclusion amount. Nothing in the Form 8938 question asks about savings bond redemptions or education expenses.

findings.situation: A filer received ordinary dividends as a nominee, answers NO because they have no foreign assets, and the tool enters the full Form 1099-DIV box 1a total on line 6.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total ordinary dividends you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 6."
findings.why: Line 6 must be reduced by nominee dividends, but the tool copies box 1a. The Form 8938 question does not identify nominee recipients.

findings.situation: A filer who is required to file Form 8938 must answer YES even though their interest and dividends are ordinary domestic amounts that the tool would put correctly on lines 2, 3 and 6.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are you required to file Form 8938 for specified foreign financial assets?"; i1040sb p. 2: "Regardless of whether you are required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR), you may be required to file Form 8938 ... with your income tax return."
findings.why: The Schedule B text treats Form 8938 only as a separate filing obligation. It does not change how lines 2, 3 or 6 are figured, so refusing these lines on a YES answer blocks amounts the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer with foreign accounts may not know whether they are "required" to file Form 8938, or may confuse that requirement with the FBAR or the line 7a foreign-account question.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Regardless of whether you are required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR), you may be required to file Form 8938" (no thresholds or definition of "specified foreign financial assets" are given)
findings.why: The Schedule B instructions do not give the Form 8938 thresholds or define "specified foreign financial assets." A filer with foreign accounts could reasonably answer either way.

question: During 2025, did you receive a distribution from a foreign trust (a loan of cash or marketable securities counts), or were you the grantor of, or a transferor to, a foreign trust that existed at any time during 2025?

findings.situation: A filer was treated as the owner of a foreign trust under the grantor trust rules without being its grantor or a transferor to it, and received no distribution from it in 2025.
findings.irs_text: "If you were treated as the owner of a foreign trust under the grantor trust rules, you are also responsible for ensuring that the foreign trust files Form 3520-A." (i1040sb TY2025, p. 3, Line 8)
findings.why: The question asks only about distributions, grantors, and transferors, so this owner can truthfully answer NO. The tool then computes the lines and never raises the Form 3520-A responsibility that its refusal is meant to route.

findings.situation: A filer received a loan of cash or marketable securities from a foreign trust that falls outside the general rule and is not considered a distribution.
findings.irs_text: Question: "a loan of cash or marketable securities counts"; IRS: "a loan of cash or marketable securities is generally considered to be a distribution. See the Instructions for Form 3520" (i1040sb TY2025, p. 3, Line 8)
findings.why: The question turns the IRS's "generally" into an unconditional rule, so this filer must answer YES and is refused. The excepted loan does not change the computed lines, which the tool could otherwise handle correctly.

findings.situation: A grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025 has no Form 3520 filing requirement for the year.
findings.irs_text: Question: "were you the grantor of, or a transferor to, a foreign trust that existed at any time during 2025?"; IRS: "If you were the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025, you may have to file Form 3520." (i1040sb TY2025, p. 3, Line 8)
findings.why: The IRS says only that such a filer "may" have to file, but the question requires YES whether or not a filing is due. The tool therefore refuses a filer with no Form 3520 obligation, even though the interest and dividend lines are unaffected.

findings.situation: A filer transferred property to a foreign trust before 2025, made no transfer during 2025, and the trust still existed during 2025.
findings.irs_text: "If you were the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025, you may have to file Form 3520." (i1040sb TY2025, p. 3, Line 8)
findings.why: The IRS text ties 2025 to the trust's existence, not to the transfer. The question's opening "During 2025" could be read to require that the filer acted as grantor or transferor in 2025, which would lead this filer to answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer who was an officer or director of a foreign corporation, or owned 10% or more of one, has a Form 5471 filing duty and answers YES to 'foreign corporation reporting', but that duty doesn't change the amounts on lines 2, 3 or 6, so the tool would compute them correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'foreign corporation reporting'. i1040sb (2025) p. 2, Part II TIP: 'You may have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you were an officer or director of a foreign corporation... or owned 10% or more...' Line 5: 'Report on line 5 all of your ordinary dividends. This amount should be shown in box 1a of your Forms 1099-DIV'
findings.why: Form 5471 is a separate information return. It doesn't adjust Schedule B line 2, 3 or 6, so asking about it refuses returns the tool handles correctly.

findings.situation: A filer who received a Form 1099-OID and is reporting exactly the box 1 or box 8 amount may read 'reported in an amount other than on Form 1099-OID' as any OID not reported on a 1099-OID, or as OID reported at a different amount. A filer whose payer already netted acquisition premium may also not know which reading applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb (2025) p. 2: 'If you are reporting OID in an amount less than the amount shown in box 1 or box 8 of Form 1099-OID, follow the rules earlier under Nominees... identify the amount to be subtracted as "OID Adjustment."'
findings.why: The phrase can mean OID that came from somewhere other than a Form 1099-OID, or OID reported at an amount different from the form. The IRS rule only covers reporting less than box 1 or box 8.

findings.situation: A filer can't tell what counts as 'other special treatment'. For example, it's unclear whether tax-exempt interest, market discount on a tax-exempt bond, or a foreign account reported on line 7a would count.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'or other special treatment?' i1040sb (2025) p. 1: 'The market discount on a tax-exempt bond is taxable interest income and not tax-exempt interest.'
findings.why: The catch-all doesn't say what it includes. One filer could answer YES for items that don't affect lines 2, 3 or 6, while another answers NO for an item that does belong on line 1 and so in line 2.

question: Do you value closing inventory by a method other than cost or lower of cost or market, or was there any change in determining quantities, costs or valuations between opening and closing inventory (line 34)? Answer No if you have no inventory

findings.situation: A filer changing their inventory accounting method beginning with 2025 refigures last year's closing inventory under the new method, so opening and closing 2025 inventory are on the same basis and the filer can truthfully answer No if the new method is cost or lower of cost or market.
findings.irs_text: If you are changing your method of accounting beginning with 2025, refigure last year's closing inventory using your new method of accounting and enter the result on line 35. If there is a difference between last year's closing inventory and the refigured amount, attach an explanation and take it into account when figuring your section 481(a) adjustment. (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Line 35)
findings.why: The question asks only about a change between opening and closing inventory, which misses a change between 2024 closing and 2025 opening inventory. The tool's input instructs the filer to enter the 2024 closing amount, rather than the refigured amount, and does not handle the explanation or section 481(a) adjustment.

findings.situation: A filer who consistently uses an IRS-approved method other than cost or lower of cost or market, with no change in method, must answer Yes even though line 35 is simply last year's closing inventory, which the tool's input takes correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Do you value closing inventory by a method other than cost or lower of cost or market"; IRS: "Your inventories can be valued at cost, the lower of cost or market, or any other method approved by the IRS." (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Line 33)
findings.why: The Line 35 text requires refiguring only when the method of accounting is changing, so consistent use of an approved other method does not make the entered amount wrong. For this line, the question refuses a case the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A small business taxpayer who chooses not to keep an inventory but holds unsold goods, or tracks them in books under a financial accounting method, could read "no inventory" as either no goods on hand or no formal inventory kept.
findings.irs_text: If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory, but you must still use a method of accounting for inventory that clearly reflects income. (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Part III, Exception for small business taxpayers)
findings.why: The wording does not say whether this filer should use the "Answer No" instruction. That choice can decide whether a filer whose treatment is neither cost nor lower of cost or market answers Yes and is refused, or answers No and has line 35 computed, possibly as zero.

findings.situation: A filer whose inventory counts or unit costs simply differ between the start and end of the year, with no change in method, could read "any change in determining quantities, costs or valuations" as covering those ordinary differences.
findings.irs_text: Question: "was there any change in determining quantities, costs or valuations between opening and closing inventory"; compare: "If you are changing your method of accounting beginning with 2025" (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Line 35)
findings.why: The question means a change in how amounts are determined, but it does not use the words "method" or "accounting method". A filer could read it as covering ordinary changes in the amounts and wrongly answer Yes, even though the tool computes line 35 correctly.

findings.situation: A filer has a non-passive loss that flows through Schedule 1, such as a sole-proprietor business or farm loss or a net operating loss carryover, but no other out-of-scope income.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p. 1, line 8: 'Additional income from Schedule 1, line 10'
findings.why: The question names 'income or loss' only for passive activities and otherwise says 'other income', so a filer with only a non-passive loss could truthfully answer NO, and line 8 would be zero. The supplied text does not include Schedule 1, so the point that line 8 can carry these losses rests on general knowledge of that schedule.

findings.situation: A filer whose only other receipts are non-taxable amounts that do not belong on Schedule 1, such as gifts, child support or life insurance proceeds, must answer YES under the literal wording, although zero on line 8 is correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'other income or return treatment outside wages, interest, dividends...'; f1040 (2025) p. 1, line 8: 'Additional income from Schedule 1, line 10'
findings.why: The question does not limit 'other income' to amounts reportable on the return, so these receipts literally fall within it. The tool would be refused for a filer whose line 8 it computes correctly. That these receipts stay off Schedule 1 rests on general tax knowledge, because the supplied text does not address them.

findings.situation: A filer with no unusual income has an item on another line the screen cites, such as a Schedule 1 adjustment, a Schedule 1-A deduction, Form 4972 tax treatment, or an adoption credit for expenses paid without employer benefits, and cannot tell whether it is 'return treatment'.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p. 1, line 10: 'Adjustments to income from Schedule 1, line 26'; p. 2, line 13b: 'Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38'; p. 2, line 16: 'Check if any from Form(s)'; p. 2, line 30: 'Refundable adoption credit from Form 8839, line 13'

findings.why: The wording excludes Schedule C and says Schedule 1-A deductions are 'asked separately', yet a NO here sets the line 5 amount to $0. Unless another screen, not shown here, catches this case, the deduction is silently lost.

findings.situation: A filer has qualified overtime included in Form 1099-NEC box 1 or Form 1099-MISC box 3, reports it on Schedule C, and answers NO because Schedule C income and Schedule 1-A deductions are carved out of the question.
findings.irs_text: 'Enter on Line 14b only the qualified overtime compensation amount that is included in Form 1099-NEC, box 1, or Form 1099-MISC, box 3.' (i1040gi 2025, p. 108)
findings.why: Nothing in the question points this filer to YES, and a NO sets line 14b to $0. Unless another screen, not shown here, catches this case, the deduction is silently lost.

findings.situation: A minister has only W-2 wages, is not filing Schedule SE because of an approved Form 4361 exemption, and must answer YES because of the phrase 'income as a minister'.
findings.irs_text: 'Check the box on line 27b if you are (1) a minister... and (2) filing Schedule SE' (i1040gi 2025, p. 43); 'Are you filing Schedule SE because you were a member of the clergy' (i1040gi 2025, p. 42, Step 5, questions 1 and 2)

findings.situation: A filer has church employee income below $108.28 and so does not file Schedule SE, but the question has no minimum amount and requires YES.

findings.why: The question 'church employee income (wages from a church that elected exemption...)' has no threshold. Below the threshold no Schedule SE is filed, so the church-employee adjustment does not arise and the wages stay in line 1z as the tool computes.

findings.situation: A filer rents out personal property as a trade or business and reports it on Schedule C, which the tool computes, but must answer YES because of the phrase 'rental of personal property'.
findings.irs_text: 'You are reporting income from the rental of personal property not used in a trade or business.' (i1040gi 2025, p. 40, Step 2, question 4)
findings.why: The question drops the IRS qualifier 'not used in a trade or business', so it reaches rental activity that the EIC test does not name. This also conflicts with the question's own carve-out for Schedule C business income.

findings.situation: An employee of a church-controlled organization, such as a school or hospital, that elected exemption from social security and Medicare taxes cannot tell whether their wages count as 'wages from a church'.
findings.irs_text: 'you had church employee income of $108.28 or more' (i1040gi 2025, p. 42, Step 5, question 1)
findings.why: The IRS text uses the broad term 'church employee income', while the question's parenthetical speaks only of 'wages from a church'. A filer employed by a separate church-controlled entity could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A clergy member or church employee paid only on Form W-2 may think their income does not require Schedule 1, because the question opens with 'Any income or adjustment requiring Schedule 1'.
findings.irs_text: 'If you are filing Schedule SE and the amount on line 2 of that schedule includes an amount that was also reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1z' (i1040gi 2025, p. 43, Clergy)
findings.why: This income is reported on line 1z and Schedule SE, not as Schedule 1 income, yet the question lists it under items 'requiring Schedule 1'. A filer could read the opening as limiting the list and answer NO, or follow the word 'including' and answer YES.

question: Do you qualify for any Schedule 1-A deduction (qualified tips, qualified overtime compensation, qualified passenger vehicle loan interest, or the enhanced deduction for a filer born before January 2, 1961), whether or not you planned to claim it?

findings.situation: A filer born before January 2, 1961 has income high enough that the enhanced senior deduction phases out to zero, so Schedule 1-A line 38 is $0. The tool's $0 on line 13b would be correct, but the filer answers YES because of their birth date.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.2, line 12d: "You: Were born before January 2, 1961"; line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: The question names the deduction as "the enhanced deduction for a filer born before January 2, 1961," so birth date alone reads as qualifying. Any filer who checks the line 12d box would answer YES and be refused, even when the Schedule 1-A amount is zero. The income phase-out itself is not in the supplied text.

findings.situation: A filer received tips (line 1c or W-2) or overtime pay but does not know whether these count as "qualified tips" or "qualified overtime compensation."
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.1, line 1c: "Tip income not reported on line 1a (see instructions)"; p.2, line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: "Qualified" is a defined term that none of the supplied text explains, so a filer with tips or overtime could reasonably answer either way. If they answer NO when the items do qualify, line 13b becomes $0 and a deduction they are owed is missed.

findings.situation: A filer meets the basic conditions for a Schedule 1-A item (tips, overtime, vehicle loan interest, or age), but the computed deduction may be limited or reduced to zero.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.2, line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: "Qualify for any Schedule 1-A deduction, whether or not you planned to claim it" can mean meeting the eligibility conditions or having a nonzero amount. Filers whose amount works out to zero could answer either way.

question: Is there a capital loss carried into 2025 from any earlier year?

findings.situation: A filer with a short-term or long-term capital gain or loss passed through on a partnership, S corporation, estate, or trust Schedule K-1, but no prior-year capital loss, truthfully answers NO, and lines 5 and 12 are entered as zero.
findings.irs_text: 5 Net short-term gain or (loss) from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts from Schedule(s) K-1 ... 12 Net long-term gain or (loss) from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts from Schedule(s) K-1 (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: The question asks only about carryovers. Pass-through capital gain or loss is a separate source that the wording never mentions, so the tool treats it as zero without refusing.

findings.situation: A filer with an installment-sale gain (Form 6252), a casualty or theft gain or loss (Form 4684), a section 1256 or straddle result (Form 6781), a like-kind exchange (Form 8824), a Form 4797 Part I gain, or undistributed long-term gain (Form 2439) truthfully answers NO, and lines 4 and 11 are entered as zero.
findings.irs_text: 4 Short-term gain from Form 6252 and short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824 ... 11 Gain from Form 4797, Part I; long-term gain from Forms 2439 and 6252; and long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824 (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: None of these sources is a carryover from an earlier year, so a truthful NO zeroes lines 4 and 11. The line labels ('zero only after unsupported source/carryover screening') assume a source screen that this question does not perform.

findings.situation: A filer had a net capital loss on the 2024 Schedule D, or negative 2024 taxable income, but does not know whether any of the loss remains after the $3,000 deduction, so cannot tell whether a loss is 'carried into 2025'.
findings.irs_text: 6 Short-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 8 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet in the instructions ... 14 Long-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 13 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: The carryover amount is the result of the worksheet, so 'is there a capital loss carried into 2025' can only be answered after the worksheet the tool declines to prepare. A filer whose prior loss may have been fully absorbed could reasonably answer either way.

question: Are there gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms 4797, 2439, 6252, 4684, 6781 or 8824, or capital gains or losses on a Schedule K-1? Count section 1256 contracts and a casualty or theft of property whether you held the property directly or through an entity.

findings.situation: A filer whose only Form 4797 amount is a loss or a gain that is not a Part I gain (for example, ordinary gain from Part II) must answer YES, although nothing from that form reaches Schedule D and the zero on line 11 is correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are there gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms 4797..."; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "Gain from Form 4797, Part I"
findings.why: Line 11 takes only gain from Form 4797, Part I, while the question counts any gain or loss on the form. The filer is refused on these Schedule D lines even though the tool's zero is correct for them.

findings.situation: A filer with a personal casualty or theft whose Form 4684 result is a loss that does not go to Schedule D, or that is not deductible, is told to count it and answers YES, although lines 4 and 11 are correctly zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Count section 1256 contracts and a casualty or theft of property whether you held the property directly or through an entity."; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 4: "short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The lines take only amounts that Form 4684 sends to Schedule D, but the question counts a casualty or theft without that limit. The routing of personal casualty losses comes from Form 4684, which is not in the supplied text, so this rests on knowledge of that form.

findings.situation: A filer with a casualty or theft that produced no gain or loss, such as one fully reimbursed at basis, cannot tell whether the event itself counts or only a resulting gain or loss.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Count ... a casualty or theft of property"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The second sentence can be read as an instruction to count every such event, or only as clarifying what counts as a gain or loss under the first sentence. The first reading gives YES and the second gives NO, and with no amount for Schedule D the correct answer is NO.

findings.situation: A filer with a fully deferred like-kind exchange on Form 8824 has a realized gain but no recognized gain, and could read "gains" either way.
findings.irs_text: Question: "gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms ... 8824"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The question does not say whether a deferred gain counts or only an amount the form carries to Schedule D. If nothing carries over, line 11 is correctly zero, but a filer could still answer YES because the deferred gain appears on the form.

findings.situation: A filer whose Schedule K-1 shows only net section 1231 gain might answer NO because the K-1 does not label it a capital gain, even if that gain belongs on Form 4797, Part I and reaches line 11.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or capital gains or losses on a Schedule K-1"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "Gain from Form 4797, Part I"
findings.why: The clause "or that belong on" Form 4797 technically requires YES, but the K-1 clause suggests that only items labeled capital count. A filer who does not know this routing could answer NO, and the tool would then wrongly treat line 11 as zero. The routing of K-1 section 1231 gain comes from text not supplied here.
